F-16 low-level flights over real terrain

The JSBSim F-16 airframe, on an AeroSim turbojet deck, flies terrain-following routes at 100 m above the ground through a Norwegian fjord and across Novaya Zemlya. Terrain heights come from Kartverket's national laser-scanned terrain model and the Copernicus 30 m elevation model. Each route is planned on those heights, and JSBSim is given the real ground height under the aircraft every step.

Lysefjorden, Norway

Kartverket 1 m laser terrain model · Mach 0.5 · 100 m set clearance
Valley route 50.0 km, lowest 98.4 m above ground; direct line 43.4 km, lowest 96.7 m.

Matochkin Shar, Novaya Zemlya

Copernicus GLO-30 elevation model · Mach 0.6 · 100 m set clearance
Valley route 118.3 km, lowest 98.9 m above ground; direct line 102.0 km, lowest 95.9 m.

How it works

  1. Terrain. Kartverket's terrain model is fetched from Geonorge's coverage service (EPSG:25833) at 20 m; Copernicus GLO-30 tiles come from the public AWS bucket. Both are resampled bilinearly onto a local transverse Mercator grid centred on the region, so x and y are true ground distances. Each tile's pixel convention (area or point) is read from the file.
  2. Ground track. The valley route is a least-cost path over the height grid. Low ground is cheap and ground near walls higher than 120 m costs extra, so the path keeps to the middle of the fjord or strait. A second-order cone programme then smooths it to the closest curve with a turn radius no tighter than 63° of bank allows at the planned speed (1.4 km at Mach 0.5, 1.9 km at Mach 0.6). The direct line joins the same end points straight across the high ground.
  3. Altitude reference. The lowest profile the aircraft can fly is a linear programme in the altitude at every 50 m. It stays at least 100 m above the highest terrain within 150 m either side of the track. Climb and dive are limited to 20° and 12°, and the curvature of the profile to a 3 g pull-up and a 0.3 g push-over. It begins each climb early enough to clear the ridge at the pull-up limit.
  4. Flight. JSBSim's F-16 is flown on AeroSim's turbojet deck, the same deck as on the main site. Every step the real terrain height under the aircraft goes to JSBSim, and the aircraft is matched to the nearest point of the route. Guidance computes one force normal to the velocity, from curvature feed-forward and cross-track feedback on the horizontal and profile tracking on the vertical. That force sets the bank angle and load factor, which the F-16's flight controls then fly.

Checking the terrain data

Over Lysefjorden the two sources are independent measurements of the same ground: Kartverket's model from airborne laser scanning, Copernicus's from TanDEM-X radar. Their difference is the check on both the data and the resampling here. Copernicus measures the surface, tree tops included, so it sits slightly higher where there is forest; above the tree line the two agree to a few metres.
